Meeting header: 2026-03-04 11:00 PST | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Alex (Orion Head of ML), Priya (CTO), Sam (SRE)

Auto-summary: quick review of this week's pilot run; main focus on tokens/sec per dollar, caching savings observed in chat prefix cache, and batching tradeoffs. Agreed to run a dedicated benchmark and share a cost model spreadsheet with scenarios.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — results recap, costs / tokens per dollar, caching effects, batching tradeoffs, and next steps. um if anyone needs different priority call it out.
[00:18] Alex: thanks maya. on our side priya and sam are with me. we ran the two baseline jobs last week — hosted smaller batch and dedicated with q4-13b quant. we wanna focus on unit economics, tokens per dollar mostly.
[00:34] Diego: cool, i'll start with the numbers we collected. caveat — some of the auto-transcripts had a couple naming glitches, but numbers are straight from the perf logs. baseline hosted (rtd instance) average throughput ~420 tokens/sec at 95ms median latency for short requests ~50 tokens. cost rate observed (hosted) roughly $0.010 per 1k tokens for the model variant we used — that maps to ~42k tokens/sec per dollar minute? sorry, to keep it simple: we computed tokens/sec per $ as a normalized metric: hosted baseline ~500 tokens/sec/$ (this is our internal normalized unit for the meeting).
[01:12] Priya: can you say that again, tokens per dollar, we need the formula you used?
[01:16] Diego: yeah, sorry. we take observed tokens/sec on a machine and divide by effective $/sec for that capacity. so example: if instance costs $3/hr and achieved 1.5k tokens/sec, that becomes (1500 tokens/sec) / (3/3600 $/sec) => 1500 / 0.000833... which ends up ~1.8M tokens/sec per dollar-hour — we normalized to tokens/sec/$ for quick comparison. i realize the unit names are confusing, we'll include the exact spreadsheet math.
[01:42] Maya: point is, dedicated runs are typically higher tokens/sec/$ due to reserved capacity. diego, what did dedicated show?
[01:50] Diego: dedicated with quantized 13B on our nvidia-a100 style nodes gave ~1,900 tokens/sec and in our cost model that's ~1,200 tokens/sec/$ (rough ballpark) given reserved pricing assumptions. with batching turned up (batch size 8) we hit bursts near 5k tokens/sec but p95 latency increased to ~420ms for single-turn queries.
[02:12] Alex: interesting — so dedicated is ~2-3x better tokens/sec/$ but adds latency risk for tail. our SLO is 300ms p95 for interactive flows.
[02:22] Sam: correct, and for risk tolerance we can't break p95 more than 10ms, so that tradeoff matters.
[02:28] Diego: right. that's where caching comes in. we tested prefix/KV caching for common first-turn prompts. once prefix cache hits, effective generated tokens drop, and per-request cost drops significantly. across our sample workload we saw cache hit rate ~36% with prefix caching, which reduced total tokens emitted by ~28% and improved cost-per-session by a similar percent. (note: hit rate varies widely by use case).
[02:56] Alex: 36% — that's higher than I expected. what's typical for a finance assistant?
[03:02] Diego: in financial QA where users ask similar account/statement questions, prefix reuse can be higher, 40-55%. for long-tail conversational threads it's lower. we used Redwood's automatic prefix detection on the sample logs you provided.
[03:16] Priya: any gotchas? e.g., state size, KV cache eviction?
[03:20] Diego: yep — KV cache pressure increases memory usage on the serving nodes. we saw eviction churn when sequence lengths for few-shot contexts exceeded 2k tokens. SRE note: that can be tuned; we have configurable TTL and per-customer cache quotas. also the transcript transcriber shows 'K V cash' sometimes, heh.
[03:40] Sam: from infra side we flagged memory for the dedicated pilot — need to provision nodes with larger GPU memory if many long seqs.
[03:48] Maya: back to batching — typical tradeoff: batching increases throughput (better tokens/$) but increases tail latency. diego, can you quantify tradeoff with numbers?
[03:58] Diego: sure. for the 13B quant run: batch=1 => 1.9k tokens/sec, p95 latency ~120ms; batch=4 => 3.6k tokens/sec, p95 ~230ms; batch=8 => 5.0k tokens/sec, p95 ~420ms. So effective tokens/sec/$ improved roughly 2.6x from batch=1 to batch=8, but p95 rose above your 300ms SLO at batch=8. batch=4 is a good middle ground for many interactive apps.
[04:28] Alex: what about real-world mixed workloads — we have some super short auth-checks and long generation tasks. how does batching handle mixture?
[04:36] Diego: dynamic batching groups similar token-length requests; short requests can be prioritized to keep latency down. Redwood supports latency-aware batching where you cap max queue time (e.g., 10ms). that reduces latency but gives up some batching gains. in our tests with max-queue=10ms and batch cap=4 we kept p95 ~210ms and saw ~1.8x throughput improvement vs no batching.
[05:02] Priya: can you quantify cost savings from caching + batching combined?
[05:06] Diego: on your sample workload: baseline hosted with no caching/batching => normalized tokens/sec/$: ~500. With prefix caching (~28% token reduction) and conservative batching (batch=4 with queue cap 10ms), we estimated combined effective tokens/sec/$ ~1,000 — roughly 2x improvement. On dedicated with quantization it was ~2,400 tokens/sec/$ with caching applied. I'll put the granular numbers into the spreadsheet.
[05:36] Sam: curious about pricing assumptions — e.g. committed reserved cluster vs on-demand instances?
[05:41] Maya: good point. our spreadsheet includes three scenarios: hosted on-demand, dedicated reserved (monthly committed), and private self-host. reserved shows best unit economics but requires commit. public hosted is best for quick tests and lower ops. private self-host gives max control but you incur infra ops.
[06:00] Alex: on security, separate thread — we still need SOC2, SAML, KMS notes. priya any comments?
[06:06] Priya: yes, our security team will want SOC2 plus audit logs for the pilot — do you have those docs?
[06:10] Maya: yes, i'll share SOC2 docs and the audit log schema. diego will attach a short runbook for KV cache encryption and KMS key rotation.
[06:18] Diego: quick note — encryption at rest for KV cache is supported; will share the KMS integration doc after this.
[06:22] Alex: thanks. returning to perf: do you have p95 numbers for the dedicated runs across larger seqs (1k-2k tokens)?
[06:30] Diego: for long seqs p95 moves up significantly: for 1k token outputs p95 was ~950ms on batch=1, and batching pushes that up further. that's why we often split streaming generation so that early tokens stream back fast and full completion cost amortized.
[06:46] Sam: any notes on streaming? we need partial results for UX to keep perceived latency low.
[06:50] Diego: streaming helps perceived latency, yes. we tested chunked streaming every 64 tokens — combination of prefix caching + streaming gives pretty snappy UX while still getting batching gains on backend.
[07:02] Alex: what's the recommended config for us given our SLO of 300ms p95 for interactive?
[07:06] Diego: recommended: dedicated reserved cluster with quantized 13B, batch cap=4, max-queue=10ms, enable prefix cache for common templates, and streaming with 64-token chunks. That keeps p95 roughly ~210-250ms in our tests.
[07:18] Priya: and cost?
[07:20] Diego: that config puts you in the ~1,800 - 2,200 tokens/sec/$ effective band after caching. We'll show scenario table with per-month estimate using your projected traffic.
[07:30] Alex: what's the simple rule of thumb we can give execs?
[07:33] Maya: dedicated reserved with caching ~2x better unit economics than hosted on-demand for steady-state high-QPS workloads; but hosted is faster to get started and has lower commitment risk.
[07:44] Alex: good. any surprises in this week's logs?
[07:47] Diego: one surprise — the cache hit distribution was skewed: 20% of users accounted for 70% of cacheable queries; if you focus on the small cohort (support flows), you get outsized benefits.
[07:58] Sam: we can prioritize onboarding that cohort first.
[08:02] Priya: how does quantization impact answer quality? we ran a couple of evals and saw minor degradation in correctness for the most precise legal wording tasks.
[08:12] Diego: correct, some regression on very precise token-level tasks. our suggestion: run quantized for general assistant flows and fall back to float variants for high-precision routes; Redwood supports automatic fallback routing.
[08:24] Alex: route-level pricing? can we mix variants and still get cost benefits?
[08:29] Maya: yes, route-level model selection: cheap quantized model for most traffic, high-precision float for a small percent — overall unit economics still favorable. We'll model that.
[08:38] Alex: ok. any blockers from your side?
[08:41] Priya: network configs for dedicated pilot — Sam is checking limits.
[08:44] Sam: yes, default egress cap might bite us during data ingest; i'll confirm details.
[08:49] Diego: i'll add notes to the runbook about socket keepalive and MTU tuning for VPC deployments.
[08:56] Maya: great, let's talk about the timeline. Diego, you said you'd run a larger dedicated benchmark?
[09:02] Diego: yes — plan to run 30-50k tokens synthetic run across 6 workers, collect p50/p95/p99, streaming latencies, and cache hit/miss breakdown. expect results by 2026-03-09.
[09:14] Alex: we'll share cleaned logs by 2026-03-05 so you can replicate with our templates.
[09:19] Priya: once we see the run, we'll decide on reserve commit size.
[09:22] Maya: wrap up, recap next steps (we'll include in the repo): share cost model, run benchmark, share SOC2 & KMS docs, and schedule ops demo.
[09:32] Alex: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[09:35] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up in email with the spreadsheet and link to the dedicated-run logs. bye.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attributions (Speaker 2/3), small OCR-like errors, some numbers paraphrased — final numbers in spreadsheet will be authoritative.

End of transcript.
